w6.title: The Human System
w6.subtitle: On-call that people survive, launches that land, and an %1% practice an organisation actually adopts.
w6.intro:
The technical practices in the previous worlds all fail the same way: a team too exhausted, too siloed or too politically weak to run them. This world covers the %1% book's Part II and Part IV: %2% design, the psychology of operational load, collaboration between %3% and product teams, launch coordination, the engagement model, and how %4% arrives in an organisation that does not have it yet. Sources: %5% book chapters 11, 28 through 33; workbook chapters 8, 11, 19, 20 and 21.

The boss is an organisational one: you are the first %6% hire at a company that thinks it wants %7%.
w6.l1.title: Being %1%
w6.l1.summary: Rotation arithmetic, operational overload, and the psychology of the pager.
w6.l1.body:
## What %2% buys

On-call is the mechanism by which a service gets a guaranteed human response within a defined time. Everything about its design follows from two constraints: the response must be fast enough to protect the %3%, and the duty must be sustainable for the people carrying it.

%1%

## The arithmetic

- **Time %4% ≤ 25%** of an engineer's time in a multi-site team (two sites, 12-hour shifts), or up to 33% at a single site. %5%'s target: no more than 25% %6% plus 25% other operational work, leaving at least 50% for engineering.
- **Team size.** To cover a 24×7 single-site rotation at 25% duty you need roughly 8 engineers; a follow-the-sun pair of sites needs about 6 per site with 12-hour shifts. Smaller than that and the rotation either burns people or leaves gaps.
- **Two engineers per shift** in many teams: a primary who takes pages and a secondary who acts as backup and handles non-urgent flow. The secondary is also the escalation path if the primary does not acknowledge.
- **Maximum two incidents per 12-hour shift.** Each incident needs time to respond, mitigate, root-cause and write up. A third leaves no time to learn, which means the same incident returns.
- **At least one incident per quarter** is a *lower* bound worth watching: a rotation that never fires produces engineers who cannot respond when it does. The fix is not to break production; it is training, %7% and wheel-of-misfortune exercises.

## Compensation and fairness

%8% compensates %9% with time off in lieu or cash, capped at a proportion of salary so managers cannot buy unlimited availability and so engineers are not incentivised to stay permanently %10%. The cap is a reliability control, not an HR detail: the incentive to reduce pages must stay stronger than the incentive to collect %11% pay.

## Feeling safe

The book is explicit that stress hormones change how people respond. Under pressure, engineers fall back on intuition and act fast; a calm engineer reasons deliberately. The practices that keep responders in the deliberate mode:

- **Clear escalation paths** and an explicit expectation that asking for help is correct behaviour.
- **Well-tested %12%** so the first move is never improvised. The book reports roughly a 3× improvement in mean time to repair when responders use %13%.
- **Blameless %14%**, so an engineer's mistake during a response is a system finding rather than a career event.
- **Practice**: drills, disaster role-play, and shadowing before a first solo shift.

The two failure modes to watch: **operational overload** (too many pages, no time to engineer) and **operational underload** (so few incidents that skills and confidence rot).

## Operational overload and the escape valve

When the pager load exceeds the team's engineering capacity, the book prescribes a sequence, not heroism:

1. Establish the data: pages per shift, actionable ratio, top sources.
2. Temporarily assign %15% to work full-time on the top sources, protected from interrupts.
3. If load stays above the cap, hand the excess back: the development team takes pages, or %16% formally hand back operational responsibility for the service.

The last step sounds drastic and is the point. An %17% team with no engineering time is an ops team, and the model has already failed.

## Shift hygiene

Handoffs are explicit and written: open incidents, ongoing risks, changes in flight, anything deliberately deferred. A shift that ends by dropping the pager is how incidents get lost between rotations.

> [aws]**On %18%.** %19% %20% %21% holds %22% schedules, escalation plans and contact channels, and can engage responders automatically from a %23% alarm; PagerDuty and Opsgenie serve the same role. Whatever the tool, encode the escalation path (primary → secondary → manager) in it rather than in people's heads, and route pages and tickets to separate destinations as in World 2. Keep %24% next to the alarm definitions in the same repository as the infrastructure code, so a new alarm without a %25% is visible in review.
w6.l1.q0.q: A single-site team wants a 24×7 rotation where each engineer is %1% no more than about 25% of the time. Roughly how many engineers does that require?
w6.l1.q0.explain: A 24×7 single-site rotation at roughly 25% duty needs about 8 engineers. Multi-site follow-the-sun needs about 6 per site with 12-hour shifts.
w6.l1.q1.q: Why does the book cap incidents at about two per 12-hour shift?
w6.l1.q1.explain: The cap protects the learning loop, not just the engineer. Without follow-up time, incidents repeat indefinitely.
w6.l1.q1.c1: Each incident needs time to respond, mitigate, root-cause and write up; beyond two there is no time to learn, so the same incidents recur
w6.l1.q2.q: A rotation has fired twice in the last eight months. What does the lesson identify as the risk?
w6.l1.q2.explain: Low page volume is good; zero practice is not. Game days, drills and wheel-of-misfortune exercises supply the missing reps.
w6.l1.q2.c0: Nothing; low page volume is the goal
w6.l1.q2.c1: Operational underload: responders lose skills and confidence, so the next real incident is handled badly
w6.l1.q3.q: Which practices help keep responders in deliberate rather than reactive thinking? Select all that apply.
w6.l1.q3.explain: Ranking responders adds exactly the stress the other practices remove, and suppresses the information %1% depend on.
w6.l1.q3.c1: Explicit permission and paths to escalate
w6.l1.q3.c3: Publicly ranking engineers by incident count
w6.l1.q4.q: An %1% team is at 80% operational load for a third consecutive month after tuning alerts. What does the book prescribe as the escape valve?
w6.l1.q4.explain: Handing load back is the mechanism that keeps the 50% cap real. A team with no engineering time has stopped being an %1% team.
w6.l1.q4.c1: Temporarily assign %1% to fix the top sources full-time, and if load stays above the cap, hand operational responsibility (or the pager) back to the development team
w6.l2.title: Communication, collaboration and the engagement model
w6.l2.summary: How %1% teams work with developers, and the %2%.
w6.l2.body:
## The relationship is the product

%1% is structurally an outsider: a team with the power to influence another team's release velocity. The book spends a full chapter on making that relationship work, because an %2% team that is resented is an %3% team that is routed around.

Mechanisms %4% uses:
- **Production meetings.** A regular, structured review of a service's recent performance: outages, paging load, %5% status, upcoming launches, capacity changes. Attended by %6% and product development together. The agenda is fixed so the meeting cannot drift into status theatre.
- **Shared ownership of the %7%.** As in World 1, a single number both teams are accountable for.
- **Embedding.** An %8% joins the development team for a quarter or two, sits with them, and works on reliability from inside. The book's guidance for the embedded %9%: start by reading the design and the %10%, find the gap between the service's needs and its instrumentation, and teach rather than fix everything personally.
- **Design consultation early.** %11% involvement at design time is cheap; %12% involvement at launch time is a negotiation.

## The engagement model: how %13% takes on a service

Not every service gets %14% support. The book describes the **Production Readiness Review** (PRR) as the gate, with several models:

1. **Simple PRR.** %15% reviews a service and takes on the pager once it meets the standard.
2. **Early engagement.** %16% joins during design, shaping the architecture before it is expensive to change. The book prefers this: the highest-leverage reliability decisions are architectural.
3. **Frameworks and platform.** Rather than reviewing every service, %17% provides a platform with reliability built in (standard serving stack, standard deployment, standard monitoring). Services that adopt it inherit the practices. This is the model that scales, and it is the direct ancestor of modern platform engineering.

## The %18%

A typical PRR checks:
- %19% and %20% defined, measured, and alerting derived from them.
- Monitoring and dashboards that answer "are we OK" and "where does it hurt".
- Playbooks for every page, and an escalation path.
- Capacity plan, including the redundancy policy and load-test results.
- Deployment: staged rollout, tested rollback, config handled as code.
- Dependencies documented with their %21%, timeouts and fallbacks.
- Data integrity: backups, tested restores, soft deletion.
- Failure modes reviewed and the biggest ones exercised.

The output is a list of required work with owners, not a pass/fail verdict delivered at launch minus one week.

## Disengagement

The book also describes %22% *leaving* a service: if a service becomes low-risk and boring, %23% hands it back and moves to higher-leverage work. Making this explicit keeps %24% capacity aimed at where it matters and removes the assumption that %25% ownership is permanent.

> [aws]**On %26%.** The "frameworks" model translates directly to a paved road: a shared %27% or %28% module set that provisions a service with %29%, %30% or %31%, the standard alarms and dashboards, deployment pipeline with %32% and rollback, log and trace wiring, and backup policy already attached. A team adopting the module inherits the PRR answers for free; the review then covers only what is unusual about the service. The %33% %34% Framework review (operational excellence and reliability pillars) is a reasonable skeleton for a PRR if you do not want to invent one, and %35% Tool tracks the findings.
w6.l2.q0.q: Which %1% engagement model does the lesson identify as the one that scales across many services?
w6.l2.q0.explain: Review and embedding are per-service and bounded by %1% headcount. A paved-road platform distributes the practices without a per-service transaction, and is the ancestor of platform engineering.
w6.l2.q0.c0: A %1% for every service before launch
w6.l2.q0.c1: Embedding an %1% in each development team
w6.l2.q0.c2: Providing a platform or framework with reliability practices built in, which services inherit by adopting it
w6.l2.q1.q: Which items belong in a %1%? Select all that apply.
w6.l2.q1.explain: A PRR checks whether the service can be operated safely. Productivity metrics have no place in it.
w6.l2.q1.c0: %1% and %2% with alerting derived from them
w6.l2.q1.c4: Lines of code written per engineer
w6.l2.q2.q: Why does the book prefer early engagement over reviewing a service shortly before launch?
w6.l2.q2.explain: A late review can only ask for cheap changes. Design-time involvement can change the failure modes themselves.
w6.l2.q2.c1: The highest-leverage reliability decisions are architectural, and changing architecture at launch minus one week is expensive or impossible
w6.l2.q3.q: What is the purpose of a regular production meeting between %1% and product development?
w6.l2.q3.explain: A fixed agenda keeps the meeting from decaying into status theatre, and the shared picture is what makes shared ownership real.
w6.l2.q3.c1: To review recent outages, paging load, %1% status, upcoming launches and capacity on a fixed agenda, so both teams share one picture of the service
w6.l2.q4.q: True or false: once an %1% team takes on a service, that ownership is permanent by design.
w6.l2.q4.explain: False. The book describes deliberate disengagement: a service that has become low-risk is handed back so %1% capacity moves to higher-leverage work.
w6.l3.title: Launch coordination and reliable product launches
w6.l3.summary: The launch checklist, the coordination engineer, and why launches deserve their own process.
w6.l3.body:
## Why launches are special

A launch changes several things at once: new code, new traffic shape, new dependencies, and often a marketing event that removes your ability to choose the timing. %1%'s Launch Coordination Engineering (LCE) exists because the failure modes of launches are consistent enough to be checklisted.

## The launch checklist

The book's checklist is the artefact worth stealing. Representative questions:

- **Architecture and dependencies.** What is the request flow? Which dependencies are in the critical path, what are their %2%, and what happens when each is slow or down?
- **Capacity.** What is the expected traffic, and where does the number come from? Has the service been load-tested to that level and beyond? What is the plan if traffic is 10× the estimate?
- **Failure modes.** What are the single points of failure? What happens when a dependency is unavailable? Is there a degraded mode?
- **Client behaviour.** Do clients retry? With backoff? Can you turn features off without a client release?
- **Process and automation.** Are manual steps required for the launch? Are they documented and tested?
- **Development process.** Is the code in version control with staged rollout and tested rollback?
- **External dependencies.** Third parties, quotas, certificates, %3% changes with long %4%.
- **Rollout plan.** Staged by percentage or region, with a defined rollback trigger and a named person who can pull it.

## Techniques the chapter emphasises

- **Feature flags / gradual ramp-up.** Decouple the code deploy from the feature launch, so the launch is a config change that can be reversed in seconds.
- **The "dark launch"**: send production traffic to the new path without showing users the results, to measure capacity and correctness under real load before the user-visible launch.
- **Kill switches** for every new feature and every expensive code path.
- **Load testing against the real dependency graph**, not against mocks that never fail.
- **Emergency contacts and a defined command structure** for launch day, because launch day incidents are incidents.

## The LCE role

A small team of launch coordinators reviews launches across the company, maintains the checklist, and carries the institutional memory of how launches fail. The value is not the gate; it is the accumulated pattern library. Where a full team is not justified, the same function can be a rotating role plus a maintained checklist.

> [aws]**On %5%.** Launch-specific items that bite: %6% (%7% concurrency, %8% instance limits, %9% throttles, SES sending limits) requested well in advance; %10% %11% lowered before a cutover and raised afterwards; %12% and %13% pre-warming considerations for extreme step changes in traffic; provisioned concurrency for %14% so the launch spike does not arrive on cold starts; %15% on-demand mode or pre-scaled provisioned capacity; and CloudFront cache behaviour verified for the new paths. Dark launch maps to shadow traffic (duplicate requests to the new stack, discard responses) or to a %16% alias receiving mirrored events. Kill switches belong in %17% feature flags, evaluated with a safe default as in World 3.
w6.l3.q0.explain: Dark launches separate "does it work at production scale" from "do users see it", so the risky question is answered first.
w6.l3.q0.c1: Sending real production traffic through the new code path without exposing results to users, to validate capacity and correctness under real load
w6.l3.q1.q: Why does the lesson recommend decoupling the code deploy from the feature launch using flags?
w6.l3.q1.explain: A flag flip is the fastest rollback available. The code can be in production, dormant and tested, before the feature is on.
w6.l3.q1.c1: The launch becomes a config change that can be reversed in seconds, rather than a deploy that must be rolled back
w6.l3.q1.c3: It avoids the need for load testing
w6.l3.q2.q: Which questions belong on a launch checklist? Select all that apply.
w6.l3.q2.explain: Traffic assumptions, dependency failure modes, rollback authority and client behaviour are the recurring launch failure modes.
w6.l3.q2.c0: What happens if traffic is 10× the estimate?
w6.l3.q2.c1: Which dependencies are in the critical path and what happens when each is down?
w6.l3.q2.c2: Who can trigger a rollback and what triggers it?
w6.l3.q2.c3: Which engineer wrote the most code for this feature?
w6.l3.q2.c4: Do clients retry, and with backoff?
w6.l3.q3.q: On %1%, which launch-day risk is best mitigated weeks in advance rather than on the day?
w6.l3.q3.explain: Quota increases are requests with lead time. Hitting a quota ceiling during a launch spike is an outage the checklist exists to prevent.
w6.l3.q3.c0: %1% such as %2% concurrency or %3% instance limits
w6.l4.title: Adopting %1% in an organisation
w6.l4.summary: Where to start, how to sequence, and the cultural changes that make it stick.
w6.l4.body:
## The starting position

Most organisations adopting %1% already have operations, alerts, incidents and unhappy engineers. The workbook's advice is to start where the pain and the leverage overlap, not to reproduce %2%'s org chart.

## A sequence that works

1. **Pick one service that matters** and that has a team willing to try. Reliability work on an unimportant service teaches nobody anything.
2. **Define one or two %3% and an %4%** for it, measured from the user's side. Publish the measurement before arguing about the target.
3. **Derive the alerting from the %5%** and delete the alerts that do not survive that test. This is usually the moment the team notices the difference.
4. **Write the %6% policy** and get it signed by someone who can enforce it. Without this, step 2 is a dashboard.
5. **Introduce blameless %7%** with explicit triggers, and share them widely.
6. **Measure %8%** and give the team protected time to remove the largest source.
7. **Then** generalise: a second service, a paved-road platform, a %9%.

The ordering matters. %10% before alerts, alerts before automation, %11% before process, and executive backing before any of it can survive contact with a launch deadline.

## Structural choices

- **Where %12% reports.** An %13% function inside the product organisation is close to the work but easy to override; one reporting into a separate engineering function has the independence to enforce a budget policy but risks becoming an outsider. The workbook's practical answer is that independence matters most for the %14% policy specifically.
- **Team topology.** Options: a central %15% team serving many services; embedded %16% inside product teams; a platform team providing the paved road; or a hybrid that starts central and spins out. Most organisations end up with a platform plus a small central group.
- **Who carries the pager.** The most common modern answer, and the one the workbook supports, is that the team that writes a service also operates it, with %17% providing the platform, the standards and help during large incidents. "You build it, you run it" with %18% support scales better than a separate team receiving other people's software.

## Culture

The workbook is blunt that the cultural changes are harder than the technical ones:

- **Blamelessness has to be demonstrated by leadership**, first time it is costly. One public search for a culprit undoes a year of %19%.
- **Reliability work must be prioritised visibly**, with the %20% as the argument. A backlog where reliability items are always below features tells the team what is actually valued.
- **Data over opinion.** Every reliability argument should be reducible to an %21%, a budget number or a page count.
- **Psychological safety** is the precondition for honest incident reporting; the workbook ties it directly to reliability outcomes.

## Measuring the adoption

Useful indicators: percentage of services with a defined and measured %22%; percentage of pages tied to an %23%; pages per shift; %24% completion and action-item closure rate; %25% percentage; time to restore (a %26% metric that overlaps neatly with %27% goals). Track the trend, not the absolute.

> [aws]**On %28%.** The paved road is the highest-leverage artefact: shared infrastructure modules that emit the standard %29%, create the burn-rate alarms, wire the deployment pipeline with %30% and rollback, attach a backup plan, and register the service in your catalogue. %31% %32% can define the %33% for services that adopt the standard instrumentation, which makes "does this service have an %34%" a query rather than a survey. Use %35% %36% and account boundaries to make the %37% of a team's mistakes their own.
w6.l4.q0.q: Put this %1% adoption sequence in the order the workbook recommends.
w6.l4.q0.explain: Measurement before targets, targets before alerts, policy before it is tested by a launch, then learning and %1% reduction. Generalising to a platform comes after this loop works once.
w6.l4.q0.i0: Pick one service that matters, with a willing team
w6.l4.q0.i1: Define and measure one or two %1% and an %2%
w6.l4.q0.i2: Derive alerting from the %1% and delete the rest
w6.l4.q0.i3: Write and get sign-off on the %1% policy
w6.l4.q0.i5: Measure %1% and protect time to remove the largest source
w6.l4.q1.q: Which statement best reflects the workbook's position on who should carry the pager for a service?
w6.l4.q1.explain: "You build it, you run it" with %1% support scales; handing software to a separate team to operate reproduces the dev/ops split %2% exists to remove.
w6.l4.q1.c0: A dedicated %1% team should receive the pager for all services
w6.l4.q1.c1: The team that writes a service should operate it, with %1% providing the platform, standards and support during large incidents
w6.l4.q1.c2: Pager duty should rotate randomly across the engineering organisation
w6.l4.q2.q: Why does the workbook argue that independence matters most specifically for the %1% policy?
w6.l4.q2.explain: Everything else in %1% can be done collaboratively. The freeze is the one moment where organisational position determines whether the policy is real.
w6.l4.q2.c0: Because budgets are a finance function
w6.l4.q2.c1: Because enforcing a launch freeze requires the ability to say no to the organisation that owns the launch
w6.l4.q3.q: Which indicators usefully measure %1% adoption? Select all that apply.
w6.l4.q3.explain: Renaming roles is the classic false signal. The rest measure whether the practices are actually operating.
w6.l4.q3.c0: Percentage of services with a measured %1%
w6.l4.q3.c1: Percentage of pages tied to an %1%
w6.l4.q4.q: A leadership team responds to a costly incident by asking who approved the change. What is the likely effect?
w6.l4.q4.explain: Blamelessness is demonstrated by leadership under cost, or it is not real. The information flow is the asset being protected.
w6.l4.q4.c1: Engineers reduce what they volunteer in future %1%, and incidents become less visible rather than less frequent
w6.l4.q4.c3: No effect if the %1% document stays blameless
w6.boss.title: First %1% Hire
w6.boss.tagline: Six months to prove the model at a company that wants the title, not the practice.
w6.boss.intro:
You are the first %1% at a 120-person company running a B2B SaaS platform on %2%. Twelve product teams, no %3%, an ops team of three that receives every alert, and a VP of Engineering who read the %4% book on holiday and wants "%5% by Q3".

Current state: about 60 pages a week across the ops team, two of whom are interviewing elsewhere. Deploys are weekly and manual. Postmortems exist as a wiki page nobody updates. You have six months and no authority over the product teams.

Health tracks both reliability outcomes and organisational credibility. Keep it above 50%.
w6.boss.win:
Six months in: one service with a real %1% and a signed budget policy, alerting that halved the pager load, a paved road four teams are adopting, and a set of metrics that measure the practice rather than the title. The ops team is doing platform work instead of receiving everyone's alerts.

**Takeaway:** %2% adoption is a sequence, not a reorganisation. Measure one thing that matters, derive the alerts from it, get the policy signed while the evidence is fresh, then build the road so the next ten teams do not need you.
w6.boss.lose:
The title arrived and the practice did not. Typical failure paths: renaming the ops team, setting the %1% to current performance, keeping all alerts centralised, missing the moment to write the budget policy, or accepting a board metric that rewards hiding incidents.

Revisit lessons 6.1 and 6.4 and retry.
w6.boss.s0.text:
The VP asks for your plan. Their proposal: rename the ops team to "%1%", give them the %2% book, and have every team file reliability tickets to them.

What do you propose instead?
w6.boss.s0.c0.text: Start with one important service and one willing team: measure two user-facing %1%, publish the numbers before arguing about targets, and use what you learn to design the wider rollout.
w6.boss.s0.c0.fb: Narrow, real and demonstrable. A measured %1% on a service that matters produces an argument nobody can wave away, and gives you a reference implementation.
w6.boss.s0.c1.text: Accept the rename and start writing standards for all twelve teams.
w6.boss.s0.c1.fb: Renaming an ops team without changing hiring, the 50% cap or shared %1% is the canonical anti-pattern. Standards written before you have measured anything have no evidence behind them.
w6.boss.s0.c2.text: Insist on hiring five more %1% before anything starts.
w6.boss.s0.c2.fb: Headcount before a working model just scales the ops team. You have not yet shown what the model does.
w6.boss.s1.text: You pick **Reports**, the service customers complain about most, and its team agrees. You measure from the %1%: 97.9% of report requests succeed within 5 s over the last 30 days. The team lead says "so our %2% is 97.9%?"
w6.boss.s1.c0.text: No: the measurement is the starting point, not the target. Ask what customers actually need, look at the complaints and the contract, then set the %1% from that and treat the gap as work.
w6.boss.s1.c0.fb: Setting the target to current performance guarantees the %1% never drives anything. The gap between need and reality is the entire value of the exercise.
w6.boss.s1.c1.text: Yes, 97.9% is a fair starting %1% since it reflects reality.
w6.boss.s1.c1.fb: An %1% that is always met by definition is a dashboard. Nobody will ever act on it.
w6.boss.s1.c2.text: Set it at 99.99% to be ambitious.
w6.boss.s1.c2.fb: A target with no path to it and no business justification gets abandoned in month two, taking the credibility of the practice with it.
w6.boss.s2.text: %1% agreed at 99.5% within 5 s. You build burn-rate alerts. The Reports team now has 3 alerts instead of 19, and the ops team asks whether they should still receive the other 16 for that service.
w6.boss.s2.c0.text: Route the %1% pages to the Reports team itself, move the rest to tickets or dashboards, and have the ops team support rather than absorb. Document the change as the template for other services.
w6.boss.s2.c0.fb: This is the pivot from "ops receives other people's alerts" to "you build it, you run it with support". Doing it on one service first makes it a demonstration rather than a decree.
w6.boss.s2.c1.text: Keep all alerts with the ops team so product teams are not disrupted.
w6.boss.s2.c1.fb: You have preserved the exact structure that produced 60 pages a week and two resignations.
w6.boss.s2.c2.fb: Some of those signals have legitimate consumers. Route them; do not silence them.
w6.boss.s3.text:
Reports has a bad month: an incident burns 70% of the budget. The Reports team proposes a fix but also has a committed customer feature. The VP asks you to decide.

There is no written %1% policy yet.
w6.boss.s3.c0.text: Use the incident as the forcing function: draft the %1% policy now, get the VP to sign it, and apply it to this decision. Reliability work takes priority while the budget is this low, with the feature scheduled immediately after.
w6.boss.s3.c0.fb: The policy is worth more than this one decision. Writing it during a real trade-off, with leadership signing, is how it acquires authority for every future one.
w6.boss.s3.c1.text: Rule that the feature ships; you have no authority to block it.
w6.boss.s3.c1.fb: You had the one moment where a policy could have been written with evidence behind it, and used it to establish that reliability loses by default.
w6.boss.s3.c2.text: Block the feature on your own authority.
w6.boss.s3.c2.fb: You do not have that authority, and exercising it without a signed policy makes %1% the department of no. The next escalation removes you from the decision entirely.
w6.boss.s4.text: Reports is stable, the policy is signed, and four other teams now want %1%. You are one person. The ops team has two people left.
w6.boss.s4.c0.text: Build the paved road: shared infrastructure modules that emit standard %1%, create burn-rate alarms, wire a %2% pipeline with rollback and attach backups. Teams adopting the module inherit the practices; you consult rather than implement.
w6.boss.s4.c0.fb: This is the frameworks model, the only one that scales past your headcount. Each adoption also answers most of a %1% for free.
w6.boss.s4.c1.text: Run a hands-on %1% project with each of the four teams sequentially.
w6.boss.s4.c1.fb: Four quarters of your time for four services, and nothing reusable at the end. Do one more if you must, then build the road.
w6.boss.s4.c2.text: Write a standards document and require every team to comply.
w6.boss.s4.c2.fb: A document with no implementation behind it converts into a compliance exercise that teams resent and route around.
w6.boss.s5.text: Review with the VP. They want a single metric to report to the board as proof that "%1% works", and suggest "number of incidents", targeting zero.
w6.boss.s5.c0.text: Offer a small set instead: percentage of services with a measured %1%, pages per shift, %2% action-item closure, and time to restore. Explain that zero incidents would mean either hidden incidents or a service too slow to change.
w6.boss.s5.c0.fb: A target of zero incidents rewards concealment and stalls delivery. A small basket of adoption and outcome measures, reported as trends, is defensible and cannot be gamed by silence.
w6.boss.s5.c1.text: Accept "number of incidents" as the metric; it is simple and the trend is down.
w6.boss.s5.c1.fb: You have just given every team a reason not to declare incidents. Within two quarters the number looks excellent and you know nothing.
w6.boss.s5.c2.text: Report %1% consumption across all services as the single number.
w6.boss.s5.c2.fb: Better than incident count, but only five services have %1%, so the aggregate is mostly noise, and it says nothing about adoption or the learning loop.
